lines.text: Every box on this shelf has a number, starting at zero.
The boxes sit side by side with no gaps. That's contiguous memory.

lines.fact: the address is computed, not searched
lines.text: I want box four. Do I open boxes zero to three first? No.
The address of box i is the base plus i times the box size.
Base 100, size 4, index 4: address 116. One multiply, one add.
So box four opens instantly, and box four thousand would too.
Same cost for any index. That's O(1) access.

lines.fact: the last valid index is length − 1
lines.text: Valid indexes run from zero to length minus one. Past that, there is no box.

quiz.q: Why does reading an array element by its index take O(1) time?
options: The address is calculated directly rather than searched for.
The computer scans through all earlier indices in parallel.
Array elements are stored in a linked hash table.
quiz.fact: Access by index is O(1) because the address is computed, not searched.

lines.text: Seats in a row, every one taken, all side by side.
A latecomer needs seat two, and everyone must stay in order.
There's no empty seat to slip into. Someone has to move.
Everyone from seat two onward shifts one seat to the right.
We move the last person first, so nobody gets sat on.
Seat two is free now. The latecomer finally sits down.

lines.fact: Insertion in the middle is O(n)
lines.text: Long row, long shuffle. Inserting in the middle costs O(n).

lines.fact: Deletion in the middle is O(n)
lines.text: Deleting is the mirror image: everyone after the gap shifts left. Also O(n).

quiz.q: Why is inserting an element in the middle of an array an O(n) operation?
options: The entire array must be reallocated in new memory each time.
All subsequent elements must shift one position to the right.
A binary search must run first to locate the slot.
quiz.fact: Insertion in the middle is O(n) because later elements must shift right.

lines.text: I'm looking for the value 54 somewhere on this shelf.
No index this time, only a value. So I have to search.
The slow way: open box after box, starting from the left.

lines.fact: one by one and is O(n)
lines.text: Worst case, I open every single box. That's O(n).
But this shelf is sorted. That changes everything.
Open the middle box: 31. Too small, so the whole left half goes.
Middle of what's left: 54. Found it in two looks.
Halving every step means about log n looks. That's binary search.
On an unsorted shelf, halving lies to you. Sort first, or search linearly.

quiz.q: What condition is required for binary search to find an element in O(log n) time?
options: The array elements must already be in sorted order.
The array length must be an exact power of two.
Every element must be stored at an even memory address.
quiz.fact: Binary search requires a sorted array and halves the search range each step, so it is O(log n).

lines.text: This row is out of order. Let's sort it with the simplest trick.
Five boxes, no plan yet. We'll only ever look at two at a time.
Compare two neighbours. If the left one is bigger, swap them.
Five and nine are already in order, so we leave them alone.
Nine meets one, then seven. Nine keeps swapping to the right.

lines.fact: largest remaining element is in its final position
lines.text: After one pass, the biggest value has bubbled to the end.
Repeat passes until nothing swaps. Up to n passes of n compares: O(n²).
Easy to write, slow when big. Fine for five boxes, not five million.

quiz.q: What is guaranteed after completing one full pass of bubble sort?
options: The entire array is completely sorted.
The smallest element has moved to index 0.
The largest remaining element is in its final position.
quiz.fact: After each bubble sort pass, the largest remaining element is in its final position.
